blocks.text: …the finest thing in the dog world
Introduction and significance 🐕

Nose work is the most comprehensive area of learning for dog owners. We will therefore provide a basic exercise guide here, which, with dedicated training, forms a very good basis for daily application that is satisfying for us and our dog.
Beyond that, the diligent dog owner can build on it, with the help of further sources of knowledge and the experience gained, and later develop their own further progress from it.
Nose work is the ultimate form of existence for our dog and describes the largest field of knowledge we encounter as dog owners and that is worth exploring.
In the constant search for a meaningful and, above all, satisfying activity with our dog, engaging with nose work as a daily practice is the most rewarding goal.
For our dog, nose work is the highest form of development on a mental and physical level and, at the same time, a very good substitute for the unwanted acting out of the prey drive.

For our dog, nose work is the highest form of development on a mental and physical level and, at the same time, a very good substitute for the unwanted acting out of the prey drive.
In the constant search for a meaningful and satisfying activity with our dog, nose work as a daily practice is the most rewarding goal.
The dog’s sense of smell 👃
Depending on the breed, the dog’s nasal mucosa contains up to 225,000,000 olfactory cells – 25 times the number found in humans.
Olfactory sensitivity to various substances is up to 1,000,000 times better than in humans.
During intensive nose work, the dog breathes in and out up to 300 times per minute.
The dog can smell in “stereo” – he is able to differentiate mixtures of scents. By means of a special palatal organ, he can convert scents into taste.
With the help of his highly sensitive whiskers, he is able to search close over surface structures even at a brisk pace without touching them or even bumping into them.
A dog is able to store an extremely large number of scent images, link this information to experiences, places and conditions, and retrieve it precisely at any time.
Why does a dog search? 🔍
The search serves solely to satisfy drives: hunting drive, prey drive, feeding drive, foraging drive, play drive and sex drive – to name the most important.
In nose work training, we primarily rely on the prey drive, the foraging drive, the play drive and the feeding drive.
We will take care to avoid appealing to the hunting drive. That remains reserved for the dog that is handled by a hunter.
The path of nose work 🌿

In nose work training there is no destination. Just as nature knows only the path with its endless possibilities, nose work too knows the path – that is, the how, at best the where to – but never arrives, because of the countless possibilities. And with that, the endless appeal of nose work with the dog has already been described.

Of course there is – indeed there must be – a goal for our dog. At the end of the search waits the thing he absolutely wants to have: his toy, his food – that is, what makes all the effort worthwhile.
Every dog owner should therefore know what their dog likes best, and make precisely this thing scarce for the dog in everyday life, so that the dog is highly motivated to search.

Remember: Nothing is more detrimental to nose work than an unmotivated, oversatiated dog with a low drive. The thing – whether toy or food – must rather be made scarce in everyday life in order to awaken the desire to find it.
What we need 🎒
Search reward – a toy or tasty food in a tin.
A search harness, which is preferable to a collar.
A search line 8 to 10 m long (our long trailing line).
Small, quickly eaten treats – such as cubes of cheese or sausage.
A starting marker – for example a stick or a small flag.
Baby powder in a shaker to determine wind direction.
The suitable training location 📍
Nose work preferably takes place in a natural environment. Our dog most likes to search in open nature. Only if necessary, or for lack of a suitable environment, do we search in an urban setting.

We should bear in mind that nose work in an urban setting means, for the dog, intensively inhaling all the gaseous substances that consumer society constantly emits. Whether this is beneficial to our friend’s health in the long run may well be strongly doubted. Therefore, practise nose work in an open, natural environment whenever possible.
Suitable for beginner dogs: meadow ground, moist and organically active soils, forest floors and wet ground without waterlogging.
Suitable for advanced dogs: ground with little or no vegetation, dry and organically poor soils, rocky surfaces, frozen ground and wet ground with waterlogging.
Procedure and objective 🐾

During our tours through the terrain, we look out for a suitable training area, check who owns it and, where necessary, obtain permission to train there with our dog. The terrain should not be heavily frequented, so that our dog does not find it too difficult at the start with the many scents. Protected areas and areas with game are off limits from the outset.

In the first weeks, we make sure that we always have the wind at our back when preparing the trail. A pinch of baby powder released from head height shows us even the slightest breath of wind. Of course, we observe in particular the behaviour of the powder close to the ground, where the dog searches.

If the wind comes from the front, our dog smells the target and will not search on the track but will rush off with his nose high. If the wind comes too strongly from the side, it pushes the still inexperienced dog off the trail – and the irritations for the dog owner would be too great.

We lay our first trail on a meadow or forest floor. The ground should be slightly moist and the vegetation not too tall. We walk at a calm, even pace and step deliberately, so that our footstep slightly opens the ground structure and releases scents. At the end of the trail, we place the search reward clearly visible on the ground.
The length of the first trails is only ten to twenty steps. The track should be simple, straight and successful. Success motivates.

We lead our dog to the starting marker, let him settle briefly, put on the search harness and give the search command – such as “Search!” – calmly and clearly. Then we let out the line. We follow him at a calm distance, without pushing, without steering, without commenting. We stay silent and observe.

When our dog finds the reward, we celebrate him exuberantly and warmly. This reward is the core of the entire training. It must be genuine, intense and immediate. In the first weeks, we lay one to two short trails daily. Regularity is decisive, not length.
Procedure and objective 📈

As soon as our dog works through the short, straight trail confidently and joyfully, we begin to extend it step by step. We first lengthen the trail to fifty, then to one hundred steps. Only when this length is managed reliably and joyfully do we introduce the first change of direction.
The first turn is a very wide, almost imperceptible curve. Only after several weeks do we work up to a distinct angle of ninety degrees.
At the same time, we begin to let the trail age: at first five, later ten, finally twenty minutes of waiting time before setting the dog on it. Over time, we extend this waiting time further.

At regular intervals along the trail, we place small intermediate finds – individual treats or small objects that the dog may indicate or pick up. These intermediate finds motivate the dog to stay on the trail and strengthen his tracking accuracy.

Particular attention is paid to our dog’s behaviour at places where the trail has been disturbed by external influences – such as game crossings, changes in ground or ground moisture. We help him only if he has really lost the trail – and even then only by calmly leading him back to the last reliable point, not by pointing or steering.

lessons.title: Exercise 3 – Lost-object search and free search

blocks.text: Procedure and objective 🌲
Once our dog has understood the basics of trail work and works reliably on simple trails, we can introduce the free search.

The lost-object search is one of the most practical applications of nose work in everyday life. We drop an object – at first a familiar toy – in the terrain without the dog noticing. Then we give the search command. Our dog gradually learns to search for lost objects on command and to retrieve or indicate them.

The free search differs from trail work in that there is no fixed starting point and no defined trail. The search reward is hidden somewhere in a limited area – at first very simply and clearly visible, later increasingly challenging.

We observe how our dog searches the terrain: whether he proceeds systematically, whether he reacts to air currents, whether he uses scent cones. With increasing experience, every dog develops his own search tactic, which we respect and train only carefully.
Procedure and objective 🏆
The person search is the supreme discipline of nose work and builds on everything learned so far.

We begin by having a person well known to the dog hide a short distance away behind a bush or tree – the dog can still almost see this. We give the search command. When the dog finds the person, he is praised effusively – and the joy of the person being searched for is at least as important as our own.

Step by step, the hiding place becomes more difficult, the distance greater, the terrain less open. The person being searched for deliberately leaves a scent trail – at first by walking calmly, later by moving briskly across country over different ground.
The person search trains the trust between dog and dog owner to an exceptional degree. Our dog learns that his nose’s judgement is always right – and we learn to trust him unconditionally.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid overtaxing. Better a shorter search completed successfully than a long, frustrating one.
Avoid impatience. Nose work takes time – for the dog and for the dog owner.
Avoid introducing difficulties too early. Each new difficulty is only introduced once the previous one is reliably mastered.
Avoid distraction. During nose work, our full attention belongs to the dog.
Avoid loud, hectic behaviour. Nose work thrives on calm, concentration and trust.
Avoid showing the dog the solution. Only a find he has worked out himself brings full satisfaction and consolidates what has been learned in the long term.
Practical impulse: Stay silent and observe

The most common mistake in nose work is intervening too much. Give your dog the command – and then: stay silent, follow, observe. Your dog knows more than you. Every well-observed search teaches you more about your dog than any correction. Trust grows through silence.
→ Is my dog motivated and hungry for his search reward?
→ Did I check the wind direction before laying the trail?
→ Is the terrain suitable for my dog’s current stage of training?
→ Do I stay calmly in the background during the search and only intervene when absolutely necessary?
→ Do I praise immediately, warmly and intensively when he makes the find?
→ Do I only increase the demands once the current stage is reliably mastered?
→ Do I train regularly – at least every second day?
→ Do I observe my dog attentively and get to know his search behaviour better and better?
→ Am I relaxed myself, and do I approach nose work with genuine joy?
→ Do I end every session with a successful find and generous praise?
